fixes.explanation: Mystery is a fair guess, because Elihu does say later that God is great, beyond our knowledge (Job 36:26). But here Elihu, the young man speaking to Job, says he will ascribe justice to his Maker (Job 36:3). He's backing God up as fair and right. Mystery is a different word, and it isn't the one Elihu uses here.

Yes, baker. Elihu says, “God rescues the afflicted by their affliction and opens their ears in oppression.” (Job 36:15). The rescue and the opened ears both come in the middle of the hard place. I'd have guessed the rescue skips the hard part, so Elihu has me checking my notes.

That would be a nice rescue, friend, the kind where the cookies never even burn. But Elihu is talking about the afflicted, people who are hurting. He says God rescues them by their affliction and opens their ears in oppression (Job 36:15). He doesn't say the rescue comes before any trouble.

A messenger is a fine idea, and it makes me think of Minty the dove, one of my cookie cutter kids, who was always passing notes down the counter. But Elihu doesn't mention a messenger here. He says God rescues the afflicted by their affliction and opens their ears in oppression (Job 36:15).

True, baker. Elihu says, “Be careful that no one lures you with riches; do not let a large bribe lead you astray.” (Job 36:18). Two warnings travel together: the lure of riches and the large bribe. Both are about being pulled off the path.

That's the point, baker. Elihu asks, “Can your wealth or all your mighty effort keep you from distress?” (Job 36:19). It's a question, and the way he puts it, the answer is no. You know when a whole paycheck disappears into one car repair? Money and hustle can't hold trouble back.

Elihu doesn't tell Job to give his wealth away here, friend. He just asks, “Can your wealth or all your mighty effort keep you from distress?” (Job 36:19). The point is that wealth and effort can't hold distress back. Nothing in the question is about the poor.

Questioning isn't what Elihu asks for here, baker. Elihu, the young man speaking to Job, says, “Remember to magnify His work, which men have praised in song.” (Job 36:24). He's calling Job to lift God's work up. A question isn't lifting anything up.

Rain it is, baker. Elihu says God draws up drops of water which distill the rain from the mist, and the clouds pour it out and shower abundantly on mankind (Job 36:27-28). So he starts with something people see all the time. Rain from the clouds is his first example.

True, baker. Elihu says, “For He says to the snow, ‘Fall on the earth,’ and to the gentle rain, ‘Pour out a mighty downpour.’” (Job 37:6). So God speaks, and the gentle rain becomes a mighty downpour. Snow and rain both answer to His word.
God, baker. Elihu says, “By the breath of God the ice is formed and the watery expanses are frozen.” (Job 37:10). So the freeze comes from His breath. Whole watery expanses, frozen by it.

Patience is a lovely word, baker, but Elihu doesn't use it in this verse. He says, “Whether for punishment or for His land, He accomplishes this in His loving devotion.” (Job 37:13). The words are loving devotion. That's what he ties to the storm.

Not quite, friend. Elihu asks, “…can you, like Him, spread out the skies, as strong as a mirror of bronze?” (Job 37:18). He's asking it as a question, and the answer he's pointing to is no. Spreading out the skies is something only God does.

True, baker. Elihu says, “Out of the north He comes in golden splendor; awesome majesty surrounds Him.” (Job 37:22). It comes right after the picture of the sun nobody can gaze at (Job 37:21). Golden splendor comes next, with awesome majesty around Him.

That's the reason, baker. Elihu says, “Therefore, men fear Him, for He is not partial to the wise in heart.” (Job 37:24). So God isn't partial to the wise in heart. That's the reason Elihu gives for why men fear Him.
